content: Obie Baizley, whose full name was William Obadiah Baizley, was born on May 25, 1917, in Montreal, Quebec, and passed away on May 3, 2000. He was a prominent politician in Manitoba, Canada, and a member of the Progressive Conservative Party of Manitoba. Baizley served as a member of the Legislative Assembly of Manitoba from 1959 to 1969. During his political career, he held cabinet positions in the governments of Dufferin Roblin and Walter Weir. Baizley received his education at Glenlawn Collegiate in St. Vital, Manitoba, and later attended the Lincoln Chiropractic College in Indiana. After completing his studies, he returned to Manitoba in 1937 and worked as a chiropractor. He also served as the president of the Manitoba Chiropractors' Association before transitioning into politics. During World War II, Baizley was a member of the Royal Canadian Air Force. In the 1959 Manitoba general election, Baizley was first elected to the Manitoba legislature. He achieved an unexpected victory by defeating Lloyd Stinson, the leader of the Manitoba Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, by a margin of 326 votes in the Osborne riding, located in south-central Winnipeg. For the next four years, Baizley served as a backbench supporter of Roblin's government. Baizley was re-elected without difficulty in the 1962 Manitoba general election. On February 27, 1963, he was appointed as the Minister of Labour in Roblin's cabinet, a position he held until September 24, 1968. At that time, he was reassigned as the Minister of Municipal Affairs. In 1967, Baizley endorsed Walter Weir to succeed Roblin as the leader of the Progressive Conservative Party. In the 1966 Manitoba general election, Baizley was re-elected with ease. However, in the 1969 Manitoba general election, he was defeated by Ian Turnbull of the Manitoba New Democratic Party by a margin of 623 votes. Following this loss, Baizley did not seek a return to political office. During the 1970s, Baizley served as the chair of the Manitoba Labour Board. Additionally, he was actively involved in his community and served as the president of Riverview United Church of Canada.
